# Education in Norway
Education in Norway dates back to as early as 2000 B.C., with cathedral schools established after 1153 to educate priests. Following the Reformation in 1537, these became Latin schools mandatory in market towns. Compulsory reading training began in 1736, and the folkeskole (primary school) was introduced in 1827, becoming mandatory for seven years by 1889 and nine years by 1969. The folkeskole was later replaced by the grunnskole ("foundation school") during the 1970s and 80s. Private schools became available under the Independent Schools Act of 2003 but remain rare compared to public schools, which dominate education under strict government regulation.
Today, the Norwegian education system is divided into three stages: elementary school (barneskole, ages 6–12), lower secondary school (ungdomsskole, ages 13–16), both compulsory and collectively called grunnskole, and upper secondary school (videregående skole, ages 16–19). Primary education emphasizes foundational skills using play and basic subjects but without official grading. Lower secondary introduces grading and elective languages or practical electives. Upper secondary offers general and vocational studies, with most students attending public schools. Norway’s education system has undergone reforms to broaden educational paths and integrate information technology, while graduation rates hover around 73%. Teachers are categorized by qualification levels, requiring university degrees and pedagogy training.
Higher education includes universities, university colleges, and private institutions overseen by the Norwegian Agency for Quality Assurance in Education (NOKUT), with admission mainly based on upper secondary school grades. Norway offers bachelor, master, and PhD degrees, with no formal division between vocational and academic higher education. Special education policies emphasize inclusive local schooling with individual support. Grading systems vary but transitioned towards the Bologna Process scales. The academic year starts mid-August with two semesters and includes national breaks and holidays. Educational quality assessments have placed Norwegian students ahead of other Scandinavian countries, though critiques exist over pedagogy and support for slower learners.
